<reason>PRO opened strongly with a vivid ambush narrative and a plausible anchoring/drip-pricing mechanism, and clarified in Rebuttal 1 that the motion means "one screen earlier," not "before any selection." But CON exploited that clarification immediately, constructing a persistent fork: either disclosure happens at first contact (menu/search), which forces worst-case estimates or bundled pricing that hurts price comparison and small sellers, or it happens merely a screen earlier (cart), which—by PRO's own anchoring logic—accomplishes little since the anchor is set earlier and the sunk-cost gap between cart and payment is trivial. PRO's attempt to escape via a "conditional policy disclosure" at the menu was clever but conceded the core point: the actual dollar figure for restaurants still isn't known until the party is seated, which CON correctly branded as posting a fee schedule rather than disclosing "all mandatory service charges" as the motion demands. PRO's closing gestured at the fork being a manufactured dilemma but never directly refuted CON's specific claim that cart-stage and payment-stage sunk costs are functionally identical, leaving that live thread unresolved in CON's favor. CON's argument was tighter, more strategically coherent across rounds, and better exploited the pressure-question exchange, giving it the clearer path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's Rebuttal 1 fork (menu-level disclosure is harmful via worst-case estimates; cart-level disclosure is useless per PRO's own anchoring logic) was the debate's decisive move—PRO never cleanly escaped it, and its Rebuttal 2 attempt to thread the needle with "conditional policy disclosure" was turned by CON into an explicit concession that the motion's literal demand (the actual charge, not a policy) is unmet for an entire business category.</best_rebuttal>
